Week 9: Testing How Far Defiance Travels

A wartime deportation law, a judge under siege, and a Chief Justice's rare rebuke defined a week measured almost to a standstill.

The week did not open with a single confrontation. It opened with the invocation of an old law that most Americans had never heard of, and it closed with the Chief Justice of the United States speaking in public defense of a judge under siege. Between those two points ran a week of ordinary-looking administrative acts. Taken together, they tested how much of the government's machinery could be bent to one branch's will. The pattern itself was not new. What changed was the openness of the defiance, and the range of institutions willing to either comply or resist.

At the close of the previous period, the Democracy Clock stood at 7:33 p.m. It closed this week at the same public time, with an internal shift of two-tenths of a minute, from 452.6 to 452.8 on the underlying scale. The number is small. It reflects a week where erosion and resistance ran close to parity. Courts blocked overreach in several major cases, even as the administration pressed forward on deportations, agency closures, and attacks on judicial independence. The clock barely moved because the week's damage was real but partly offset by rulings that held the line, at least for now.

The week's spine was a single legal document from 1798. The administration invoked the Alien Enemies Act to deport more than two hundred Venezuelan and Salvadoran men, mostly on the strength of tattoos and social media posts, without hearings of any kind. Judge James Boasberg issued a temporary restraining order the same day, trying to halt the flights before they landed. The planes did not turn back. A senior Justice Department official reportedly told colleagues to consider proceeding regardless of the court's order. This was not confusion about timing. It was a choice to test whether a judge's word still bound the executive once the wheels were in the air.

The consequences of that choice fell on real people. Kilmar Ábrego García, a Maryland resident with protected legal status, was swept into the same operation and sent to a Salvadoran mega-prison, an error the government would later call administrative. Others were deported on evidence as thin as a crown tattoo or a photograph of a toy water pistol. A gay makeup artist with no criminal record ended up in the same prison. His case, his lawyers said, rested on symbols badly misread. These were not isolated mistakes. They were the visible edge of a system that had traded due process for speed, and speed produced casualties.

The reach of enforcement extended past deportation cases into speech itself. Mahmoud Khalil, a green card holder, was arrested over pro-Palestinian campus activism, reportedly after a private advocacy group submitted his name to the government. Georgetown researcher Badar Khan Suri was detained for family ties and social media posts. Immigration advocate Jeanette Vizguerra was picked up outside a store in Colorado. Secretary of State Rubio warned that anyone joining what he called "pro-terror riots" would be denied visas. None of this required new legislation. It required only a willingness to turn existing immigration authority against protected expression, and that willingness was on clear display.

The scale of the immigration actions widened further by week's end. DHS revoked temporary protected status for more than 530,000 people from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, exposing them to removal with little notice. More than a thousand international students had their visas terminated, often for reasons the government did not explain. Lawsuits followed quickly. But the administrative machinery had already moved. For a large number of people, citizenship and lawful presence had become something withdrawn by memo rather than defended in court first.

The confrontation with the judiciary reached its sharpest point over Judge Boasberg himself. After his restraining order, Attorney General Bondi accused him publicly of favoring terrorists. Trump called for his impeachment. Elon Musk amplified the demand and donated to members of Congress who supported it. A House member filed formal impeachment articles. The administration simultaneously sought to have Boasberg removed from the case entirely rather than comply with his ruling. Chief Justice Roberts felt compelled to respond in public, saying impeachment is not the answer to a disputed ruling. That alone was rare. By week's end, reports described threats against the judge's family. The message to every other judge in the country was unmistakable: rule against this administration, and expect to become a target, not just a name on a docket.

Alongside the attack on Boasberg, Trump praised Judge Aileen Cannon during a speech at the Justice Department, holding her up as a model of judicial conduct. The contrast was not subtle. Judges who ruled favorably were held as exemplars. Judges who ruled against the administration were called partisan actors deserving removal. This is not disagreement with outcomes. It is an attempt to make judicial loyalty, not judicial reasoning, the measure of legitimacy.

Two major institutions were dismantled by executive order rather than by Congress. Voice of America and its sister broadcasters, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and Radio Free Asia, were defunded, placing more than 1,300 journalists on leave in a single stroke. The Department of Education was targeted for effective closure through an order directing its dismantling. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general moved swiftly to challenge it in court. Congress created both institutions and funds them by law. Neither was closed by legislative repeal. Both were hollowed out by an order signed at a desk.

Pressure on institutions extended into coercion of private actors who might otherwise resist. The law firm Paul Weiss was targeted by executive order, then released from it only after agreeing to provide forty million dollars in pro bono legal services and abandoning its diversity programs. The administration also directed the Attorney General to refer lawsuits against the government to the White House and to recommend sanctions against the attorneys who filed them. Columbia University lost 400 million dollars in federal funding over allegations tied to campus protest response. The University of Pennsylvania lost 175 million dollars over transgender athlete policy. Whatever the merits of any single dispute, the pattern showed federal money and legal threat used as instruments of compliance, not tools of policy debate.

Civil courts did their own work in the same direction. A North Dakota jury ordered Greenpeace to pay Energy Transfer more than 660 million dollars over its role in pipeline protests. Many read the verdict as a warning to future activists about the financial risk of organized dissent. No government order was needed here. The private civil system supplied its own chilling effect, at a scale most protest movements could not survive.

Not every front moved toward consolidation. Federal judges pushed back with real effect this week. Judge Theodore Chuang found that the dismantling of USAID likely violated the Constitution. Judge Ellen Lipton Hollander blocked the DOGE team's access to Social Security data covering nearly seventy million beneficiaries, calling the effort a fishing expedition. A separate judge blocked the administration's transgender military ban. Another blocked a large clawback of climate grant funding. These were not symbolic gestures. They stopped or slowed real actions, at least temporarily, and showed that judicial resistance remained functional even under direct political attack.

The response to one of those rulings revealed something about the temperature of the moment. After Judge Hollander's order limiting DOGE's access to Social Security data, the agency's acting commissioner, Leland Dudek, threatened to shut down the entire agency rather than comply, as he put it. The judge issued clarification letters correcting his account of what her order actually required. It is a small episode. But it captures a broader pattern: officials meeting judicial constraint not with compliance but with threats built to make compliance look like disaster, daring the public to blame the court instead of the agency.

Ethical guardrails around senior officials frayed in smaller, quieter ways. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick urged television viewers to buy Tesla stock, a company tied to one of the administration's most influential advisers. Trump himself acknowledged that Elon Musk should not see certain plans regarding China, given his business interests, a rare admission that raised more questions than it answered about what Musk had already seen. Defense Secretary Hegseth's earlier disclosure of classified strike details on an unsecured messaging app remained unresolved, its consequences deferred rather than delivered. None of these episodes carried the weight of the deportation flights or the attack on Boasberg. Together they described an environment where personal enrichment and private access moved easily alongside official duty, largely without cost.

The federal student loan program, covering 1.7 trillion dollars and 42 million borrowers, was transferred to the Small Business Administration. That agency announced a 43 percent workforce reduction on the same day it took on the portfolio. Whatever the intent, the practical effect was to hand a program touching tens of millions of households to an agency stripped of the staff needed to run it. Officials framed this as efficiency. It reads, in the record, as a significant risk absorbed by borrowers who had no say in the decision.

Historical memory took its own small hits. A Pentagon webpage honoring a Black Medal of Honor recipient was removed, its URL altered to include the letters "DEI," before public outcry forced its restoration. Air Force training material featuring the Tuskegee Airmen and the Women Airforce Service Pilots was pulled. These reversals suggest the erasures were not fully planned, or not fully defended once exposed. But the fact that such material was removed at all, even briefly, shows how readily institutional memory can be treated as expendable when it collides with a political mood.

Congress, for its part, mostly moved in step with the executive rather than against it. House Republicans passed a partisan funding measure without Democratic input. A member of that same chamber filed the impeachment articles against Boasberg. The legislative branch holds the plainest constitutional tools to check executive overreach. It spent the week largely occupied with amplifying it instead.

By the close of the week, the pattern was not one of sudden capture. It was one of testing, on many fronts at once, how far executive will could travel before something stopped it. Some things stopped it: judges kept ruling, attorneys general kept filing, a Chief Justice broke his usual silence. Other things did not: deportation flights proceeded, agencies closed by memo, and a judge's family reportedly faced threats over a ruling made in the ordinary course of his job. The clock's near standstill reflects that balance. It does not reflect calm. It reflects a system straining in two directions at once, with neither side yet strong enough to settle the matter.
